purpose: The quantitative core of home baking: expressing any recipe in baker's percentages on a flour=100 basis, auditing it against hydration/fat/sugar/salt/leavening budget bands with hidden water made explicit, converting mass to pan depth via density priors and pan geometry, scaling bake time near-linearly with depth under an internal-temperature doneness override, and closing every budget after swaps, dietary constraints, tiering, and process loss.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors
masses are in grams and are the ground truth; volumes are conveniences to be converted before any math
a US large egg is 50 g shelled (about 30 g white, 19 g yolk); one cup is 236.6 mL; one teaspoon is 4.93 mL
home-oven, sea-level context: conventional bake, standard pan alloys, no combi/steam control
density priors describe conventionally mixed batters and doughs (creamed, foam, straight-dough) at the moment of panning
exclusions: flavor pairing, sensory design, and ingredient selection rationale — owned by a sibling culinary KB
yeast fermentation scheduling, sourdough microbiology, and proof time-temperature tables; this KB only books preferment flour and water into the ledger
high-altitude adjustment tables (above about 900 m the leavening and liquid corrections need their own model)
oven heat-transfer engineering (convection coefficients, radiation view factors) beyond the empirical depth exponent bounds
nutrition labeling, calorie math, and food-safety pathogen modeling beyond internal doneness temperatures

competency_questions.question: How is an arbitrary home recipe restated in baker's percentages, and what is the flour basis when several flours, cocoa, or a preferment are present?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: answer divides every ingredient mass by total flour mass x 100, sums all flours plus cocoa into the basis, books preferment flour into the total (a 100 g flour poolish inside a 500 g flour dough leaves 400 g to add), and shows one worked line such as 50 g egg on 250 g flour = 20%

competency_questions.question: How much hidden water do eggs, dairy, butter, and fruit purees contribute to a formula?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: answer applies the constants (egg 75%, milk 87-88%, butter 16%, banana about 75%, applesauce about 88%) and computes a case such as 50 g egg on 250 g flour = 37.5 g water = 15% hydration-equivalent

competency_questions.question: Is a given formula's total hydration inside the band for its product class, and how is the full budget audit run?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: answer classifies the product, sums added plus hidden water, and compares to the class band (pour batters about 95-110%, lean bread 60-75%), e.g. a 1-2-3-4 cake audits to 396 g water on 360 g flour = 110%, at the top of band

competency_questions.question: How is the 3-4% chemical leavening budget split between baking soda and baking powder given the formula's acidity?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: answer allocates soda first to acid (about 2.3 g soda per 245 g buttermilk), converts soda to powder-equivalent at 1 g soda = 3-3.5 g powder, and tops up with powder to land total lift in the 3-4%-of-flour band

competency_questions.question: What are the correct salt, fat, and sugar dosing bands, and how do volume measures silently corrupt them?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: answer states salt 1.8-2.2% of flour and shows the crystal trap (2 tsp Diamond Crystal kosher = 5.6 g = 1.1% on 500 g flour, under band; 2 tsp table salt = 12 g = 2.4%, over band) plus class fat/sugar bands with one computed check

competency_questions.question: Given a batter mass, pan dimensions, and a density prior, what depth and fill fraction result, and does the batter fit?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: answer computes depth from mass, pan dims, and a stated density prior — e.g. 800 g creamed batter at 0.9 g/mL in an 8-in round (area 324 cm^2) gives 889 mL, 2.7 cm depth, 54% fill of a 5.1 cm pan — and compares fill to the class ceiling

competency_questions.question: How is a recipe rescaled between pans of different size or shape?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: answer scales by area ratio at constant depth (8-in to 9-in round = (4.5/4)^2 = 1.27x; 9-in to 8-in = 0.79x) or by volume ratio when depth must change, and says which bake-time consequence follows

competency_questions.question: How does bake time change when batter depth changes, and what actually decides doneness?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: answer scales time by depth^0.8-1.1 (doubling depth gives 1.7-2.1x time, never the 2x-per-volume intuition on width changes), and subordinates the estimate to an internal-temperature target such as 93-99 C for butter cakes

competency_questions.question: How are the budgets re-closed after an ingredient swap such as honey for sugar or buttermilk for milk?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: answer runs the closure ledger: 120 g honey replacing 100 g sugar imports about 20 g water so added liquid drops 20 g; milk to buttermilk moves about 2.3 g of lift per 245 g from powder to soda; every touched band is re-checked

competency_questions.question: How does an eggless constraint change the water ceiling and the substitution arithmetic?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: answer replaces each 50 g egg's 37.5 g water explicitly, tightens the class hydration ceiling by 5-10 points because no egg protein sets the crumb, and adds a binder (7 g flax + 45 g water per egg) with its own water booked

competency_questions.question: How much batter does each tier of a 6/8/10-in tier cake need at equal depth?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: answer uses area ratios 36:64:100, e.g. at 2.7 cm depth and 0.9 g/mL the layers take about 443/788/1231 g, and notes the 6-in plus 8-in together equal one 10-in (36+64=100)

competency_questions.question: How much dough or batter must be mixed to hit a target baked mass given process losses?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: answer divides target by (1 - loss fraction): a 900 g baked loaf at 12% bake loss needs 900/0.88 = 1023 g dough, plus 2-4% bowl/transfer residue on top

competency_questions.question: How is a density prior verified before committing a batter to a pan?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: answer runs the cup test — weigh the same cup filled with batter and with water, SG = batter mass / water mass — and states that a measured SG (e.g. 0.88 vs an assumed 0.95) replaces the prior in all depth and fill math

glossary.definition: The convention that total flour mass is 100% and every other ingredient is expressed as (its mass / total flour mass) x 100, so formulas scale linearly and compare across batch sizes; 50 g egg on 250 g flour is 20% egg.

The denominator of all percentages: the sum of every flour in the formula, including flour inside a preferment and (by this KB's convention) cocoa powder, since cocoa absorbs water like flour; get the basis wrong and every percentage downstream is wrong.

All water in the formula — added water plus the hidden water inside eggs, dairy, butter, and purees — expressed as a percent of the flour basis; pour batters run about 95-110%, lean bread dough 60-75%.

Water carried inside wet ingredients rather than added as water: egg is about 75% water, milk 87-88%, butter about 16%, banana puree about 75%, applesauce about 88%; it must be booked or the hydration budget silently overruns.

The acceptable range for a formula lever expressed in baker's percent — e.g. salt 1.8-2.2%, chemical leavening 3-4% powder-equivalent, pour-batter hydration 95-110% — used as a pass/flag audit gate rather than a hard law.
A default mass-per-volume for a batter class used to convert mass to pan volume before anything is baked: creamed cake 0.85-1.0 g/mL, foam/sponge 0.45-0.6, bread dough 1.1-1.2, cookie dough 1.0-1.1.

Batter density relative to water, measured by weighing one cup of batter and one cup of water in the same cup (SG = batter mass / water mass); the cheap measurement that verifies or replaces a density prior.
Panned batter volume divided by pan brim volume; class ceilings (creamed cakes 1/2-2/3, muffins 2/3-3/4, foam cakes in ungreased tube pans up to 3/4) leave headroom for the 1.5-2x rise.
Mass lost to evaporation during baking, typically 10-15% for pan loaves and 8-12% for cakes; yield planning divides the target baked mass by (1 - loss) to size the raw batch.

The bookkeeping run after any ingredient swap: list what mass of water, fat, sugar, salt, and acid the swap adds and removes, then adjust other lines until every budget band is back in range before baking.

nodes.definition: Express every ingredient as a percent of total flour mass with flour fixed at 100: percent_i = (mass_i / total flour mass) x 100. On 250 g flour, 50 g egg is 20% egg, 5 g salt is 2%, 175 g water is 70% hydration. The convention makes formulas scale-free (a 2% salt line is correct at 250 g or 2.5 kg flour), lets budget bands be stated once for all batch sizes, and turns recipe comparison into a column-by-column diff. Percentages routinely exceed 100 (sugar in high-ratio cakes, fruit in heavy quick breads); that is a feature, not an error. All downstream budget, swap, and audit math in this KB is stated in these units, so this convention is the load-bearing floor of the whole graph.

excluded: which mass counts as flour (flour basis rules)

pros.claim: Scale-free percentages let one band statement govern every batch size without re-derivation
pros.example: salt at 2% is 5 g on 250 g flour and 50 g on 2.5 kg flour with no new arithmetic

pros.claim: Percent columns expose formula family membership at a glance
pros.example: seeing 100% butter / 100% sugar / 100% egg instantly identifies a pound cake before reading the title

cons.claim: The convention has no denominator for flourless products, so it silently fails exactly where home bakers still want math
cons.example: a 6-egg flourless chocolate torte or a meringue has zero flour, and percent-of-flour returns division by zero unless a stated fallback basis (egg mass or total mass) is declared

cons.claim: Percent-of-flour hides absolute quantities that matter at tiny scale
cons.example: 0.9% soda on 120 g flour is 1.1 g, below what a typical home 1 g-resolution scale can dose reliably, yet the percentage looks unremarkable

failure_modes: computing percentages against total recipe mass instead of flour mass, which shrinks every number and makes bands unusable
quoting hydration without stating the flour basis, so 70% on all-purpose reads identical to 70% on a basis that omitted the preferment flour
acceptance_tests: given a full gram-weight recipe, the restatement divides each line by total flour and reproduces 50 g egg on 250 g flour = 20% and 175 g water = 70%
revisit_triggers: a flourless or near-flourless product family enters scope and needs a declared fallback denominator
a downstream node starts quoting percentages against a basis other than total flour

base.update_signal: a product family emerges where the flour denominator is absent or ambiguous, forcing a documented fallback basis

nodes.definition: Define exactly what sums to 100: all flours are added into one basis (a 200 g bread flour + 50 g whole wheat dough has a 250 g basis, so 175 g water is 70%, not 87.5% on bread flour alone); flour inside a preferment counts in the total (a poolish of 100 g flour + 100 g water inside a 500 g flour, 70% dough means 350 g total water, of which 100 g already sits in the poolish, leaving 250 g to add); and cocoa powder is booked into the basis by convention here because it absorbs water like flour (a 250 g flour + 40 g cocoa cake has a 290 g basis). Whole-grain flours absorb 5-10 hydration points more than white flour at equal handling, so a same-percent whole-wheat swap behaves drier — record the shift, do not re-guess it later.

pros.claim: A single declared basis makes hydration comparable across plain, whole-grain, and chocolate versions of one recipe
pros.example: the chocolate variant at 290 g basis and the plain at 250 g basis can both be audited against the same 95-110% pour-batter band

pros.claim: Booking preferment flour prevents double-hydrating the final dough
pros.example: forgetting the poolish's 100 g water and adding the full 350 g yields 90% real hydration on a dough designed for 70%

cons.claim: The cocoa-in-basis convention is not universal, so formulas imported from sources that exclude cocoa read 10-16 points wetter here than their authors intended
cons.example: a published 100% hydration chocolate cake computed on flour-only re-audits to 86% on a 290 g flour+cocoa basis and gets wrongly flagged as under-hydrated

cons.claim: Absorption offsets for whole grains are flour-lot dependent and drift
cons.example: a coarse stone-ground whole wheat can want +10 points where a fine roller-milled one wants +5, off one bag's protein and bran spec

failure_modes: computing hydration on white flour only and ignoring the whole-wheat share, understating real hydration
counting preferment water but not preferment flour, inflating apparent hydration by the preferment's percentage
acceptance_tests: the poolish worked example closes: 500 g total flour, 70% hydration, 100 g flour + 100 g water preferment leaves exactly 400 g flour and 250 g water to add
revisit_triggers: a formula imports from a source using a flour-only basis with cocoa excluded
a new absorbent dry (almond flour, oat flour, malted grain) needs an in-or-out ruling

base.update_signal: a new dry ingredient class needs an in-basis or out-of-basis ruling, or the cocoa convention conflicts with a major source

nodes.definition: Convert every volume line to grams before any percentage math, using method-aware constants: flour 120-125 g per cup spooned-and-leveled but 140-150 g scooped (a +17-25% silent error), granulated sugar 200 g/cup, packed brown sugar 213-220 g/cup, butter 227 g/cup (113 g per stick), water/milk 237-240 g/cup, honey 340 g/cup, cocoa 85 g/cup, and salt by crystal: table salt about 6 g/tsp, Morton kosher about 4.8 g/tsp, Diamond Crystal kosher about 2.8 g/tsp — the same '1 tsp salt' spans a 2.1x range. Eggs convert by count: large = 50 g shelled (white 30 g, yolk 19 g). The conversion is the single largest error source between a written home recipe and its real formula, so it runs first and its assumptions (spooned vs scooped, salt brand) are recorded on the ledger.

pros.claim: Method-aware constants recover the author's intended formula instead of the reader's cup technique
pros.example: a 1955 recipe assuming scooped flour at 145 g/cup re-audits correctly instead of reading 20% drier when converted at 120 g/cup

pros.claim: Converting once up front makes every later band check pure arithmetic
pros.example: after conversion, the salt line is 9 g on 450 g flour = 2.0% with no unit reasoning left to do mid-audit

cons.claim: Published cup weights for flour genuinely disagree by source, so any single constant misstates some recipes
cons.example: King Arthur uses 120 g/cup while USDA lists 125 g and many test kitchens assume 130-142 g; a 3-cup recipe spans 360-426 g depending on which author wrote it

cons.claim: Count-based egg conversion breaks on non-large eggs
cons.example: three jumbo eggs are about 189 g, not 150 g — a hidden +29 g water (about 12 hydration points on 250 g flour) that the count rule never sees

failure_modes: converting salt volume with the wrong crystal constant and dosing half or double the band
applying the spooned flour constant to a recipe written for scooped cups, shifting apparent hydration by up to 25%
acceptance_tests: a conversion pass leaves no volume-only lines and reproduces the crystal check: 2 tsp Diamond Crystal = 5.6 g but 2 tsp table salt = 12 g
flour converted both spooned (120 g/cup) and scooped (145 g/cup) brackets the formula and the chosen assumption is recorded
revisit_triggers: a recipe source declares its own cup weight standard
a salt brand change invalidates the recorded g/tsp constant

base.update_signal: a measured cup-weight or g/tsp constant for a staple ingredient shifts by more than 5% from the table value

nodes.definition: Classify the product before judging any number, because every band and prior is class-conditional: lean bread dough (hydration 60-75%, fat 0-2%, sugar 0-2%, density 1.1-1.2 g/mL), enriched dough (hydration 55-70% with milk/egg water counted, fat 10-25%, sugar 10-25%), pour batters — layer cakes, pancakes (total hydration about 95-110% including hidden water, butter 50-70%, sugar 80-110%), drop batters — muffins, quick breads (hydration 80-105%, fat 30-60%, sugar 40-70%), cookie dough (hydration 10-25%, butter 50-65%, sugar 60-100%, density 1.0-1.1), and foam/sponge cakes (egg-structured, density 0.45-0.6 g/mL, fat 0-25%). The class is decided from structure-setter and mixing method, not the recipe title: a 'bread' sweetened to 40% sugar with 100% hydration is a drop batter and must be judged as one.

included: the six product classes and their band sets
classification by structure-setter and mixing method
class-conditional density priors and doneness targets
excluded: laminated pastry and choux (out-of-band special families)

pros.claim: Class-conditional bands stop false alarms that a single universal band would raise constantly
pros.example: 107% sugar is normal for a chocolate chip cookie and catastrophic for a lean baguette; one global sugar band cannot serve both

pros.claim: Classification by structure-setter catches mislabeled recipes before their bands mislead
pros.example: a 'banana bread' at 100% hydration and 45% sugar audits sanely as a drop batter instead of failing every bread band

cons.claim: Hybrid products sit between classes and inherit two contradictory band sets
cons.example: brioche at 50% butter is scored under-fat by cake bands and over-fat by enriched-dough bands; the class call itself becomes the disputed variable

cons.claim: Six classes cannot span real home baking's tail
cons.example: choux paste (hydration about 150%, egg-set, twice-cooked) matches no class, and forcing it into pour-batter bands flags every line

failure_modes: auditing a foam cake against creamed-cake density (0.9 vs 0.5 g/mL) and sizing the pan at half the needed volume
letting the recipe title pick the class so a sweet quick bread gets judged by lean-bread hydration
acceptance_tests: given five gram-weight formulas without titles, classification lands each in the class whose full band set it satisfies, and declares any no-fit formula out of scope instead of forcing it
revisit_triggers: a recurring product (choux, laminated, flourless) needs a seventh class rather than a forced fit
a class band is contradicted by three or more trusted formulas in a row

base.update_signal: a product family recurs that no existing class fits, or a band edge is falsified by repeated trusted formulas

nodes.definition: Book the water hiding inside wet ingredients using standing constants: whole egg about 75% water (a 50 g egg carries 37.5 g; white about 90% so 30 g white carries 27 g; yolk about 50% so 19 g yolk carries 9.5 g), milk and buttermilk 87-88% (240 g milk carries about 210 g), yogurt about 85%, butter about 16% (100 g butter carries 16 g water and about 81 g fat), honey about 17%, banana puree about 75%, applesauce about 88%, pumpkin puree about 90%. Worked anchor: 50 g egg on 250 g flour is 20% egg but only 15% hydration-equivalent (37.5/250). These constants are what make the total-hydration budget computable at all: a formula with zero added water can still stand at 110% hydration entirely from eggs, milk, butter, and fruit.

included: water-fraction constants for eggs, dairy, fats, sweeteners, purees
hydration-equivalent conversion of any wet ingredient
excluded: the band judgment itself (owned by the hydration budget)

pros.claim: Constants turn invisible liquid into auditable lines, catching wet formulas that list no water at all
pros.example: a banana loaf with 300 g banana, 100 g butter, and 100 g egg shows 225 + 16 + 75 = 316 g hidden water before a single gram is poured

pros.claim: Part-level egg constants make white/yolk reformulations exact
pros.example: swapping 2 whole eggs (75 g water) for 3 whites plus 1 yolk (90 g white water + 9.5 g yolk water = about 90.5... computed as 81 + 9.5 = 90.5 g) books a +15.5 g water shift instead of assuming egg-for-egg neutrality

cons.claim: Produce constants have real biological variance the table cannot see
cons.example: a barely ripe banana runs near 70% water while an overripe black-skinned one approaches 78%, a 24 g swing on 300 g of banana — about 10 hydration points on 250 g flour

cons.claim: Butter's water fraction varies by legal standard and brand
cons.example: European-style butter at 82-84% fat carries 14-15% water vs 16-18% for standard US butter, so a 200 g butter formula shifts about 5 g of water on a brand change

failure_modes: counting only added water so a milk-and-egg cake audits 60 points below its real hydration
double-booking (adding the egg's mass to the liquid line and also applying the 75% constant)
acceptance_tests: the anchor computes: 50 g egg on 250 g flour = 37.5 g water = 15% hydration-equivalent
a zero-added-water formula's hidden-water sum reproduces within 2 points when recomputed independently
revisit_triggers: a formula leans on a puree or dairy item not in the table
a bake result implies a constant is off by more than 5 percentage points for a named brand

base.update_signal: a measured water fraction for a staple wet ingredient departs from the table by more than 5 percentage points

nodes.definition: Sum added water plus all hidden water on the flour basis and compare to the class band: pour batters about 95-110%, drop batters 80-105%, lean bread 60-75%, enriched dough 55-70%, cookie dough 10-25%. Worked closure: a 1-2-3-4 cake (360 g flour, 227 g butter, 400 g sugar, 200 g egg, 240 g milk) hides 227x0.16 + 200x0.75 + 240x0.875 = 36.3 + 150 + 210 = 396.3 g water = 110% of flour — at the top of the pour-batter band, so any wet swap must be offset gram-for-gram or the formula exits band. Sugar above about 100% additionally liquefies the batter at oven temperature (dissolved sugar acts as liquid), so a top-of-band hydration plus top-of-band sugar is flagged even though each band individually passes.

excluded: gluten development mechanics beyond absorption offsets

pros.claim: A single closed number predicts wet failures before the oven does
pros.example: the banana-loaf audit showing 128% hydration on a drop-batter band capped at 105% predicts the sunken gummy center that two test loaves later confirmed

pros.claim: Band position, not just pass/fail, prices how much swap headroom exists
pros.example: the 1-2-3-4 cake at 110% has zero wet headroom, so a honey swap must surrender 20 g of milk to stay closed

cons.claim: Hydration alone cannot distinguish free water from bound water, so two in-band formulas can behave oppositely
cons.example: 100% hydration delivered as milk (with 3.3% casein and lactose binding water) bakes noticeably drier than 100% delivered as plain water, yet the budget scores them identical

cons.claim: Bands assume standard white-flour absorption and mislead on absorbent bases
cons.example: a 100% whole-wheat pour batter at 108% hydration behaves like a white-flour batter at about 100% because bran binds the difference

failure_modes: passing a formula on added water alone while hidden water pushes it 30+ points over band
treating the band as a target and 'correcting' a proven heirloom recipe to band center without being asked
acceptance_tests: the 1-2-3-4 audit reproduces 396 g / 360 g = 110% within a point
for any pass verdict, an independent re-sum of hidden water changes the verdict in fewer than 1 in 20 cases
revisit_triggers: a swap or dietary constraint touches any wet ingredient
the flour basis changes (cocoa added, whole-grain share shifts)

base.update_signal: repeated bakes show a class band edge is mis-set by more than 5 points, or free-vs-bound water starts driving verdicts

nodes.definition: Dose tenderizers by class band, quoting the carrier and the pure fat separately (butter is about 80-82% fat, so 63% butter = about 51% pure fat): butter cakes run butter 50-70% and sugar 80-110% of flour; pound cake sits at the 100/100/100/100 corner; high-ratio cakes carry sugar 110-125% but only with emulsifier-bearing shortening and two-stage mixing — reaching for 120% sugar with plain butter and creaming is a known collapse formula; cookies run butter 50-65% and sugar 60-100% (a classic chocolate chip at 280 g flour, 227 g butter, 300 g sugars audits to 81% butter — deliberately over band, which is why it spreads flat); muffins 30-60% fat and 40-70% sugar; enriched breads 10-25% each; lean breads 0-2%. Sugar and fat trade against structure: each 10-point sugar increase visibly weakens set, so the budget is judged jointly with hydration, never alone.

included: fat and sugar bands per class

pros.claim: Joint fat/sugar accounting explains texture outcomes that single-lever reasoning misreads
pros.example: a cookie spreading into lace is diagnosed as 81% butter + 107% sugar acting together, not as an oven-temperature fault

pros.claim: The high-ratio precondition blocks a specific, expensive failure
pros.example: flagging 120% sugar with plain creamed butter predicts the sunken wet-band cake before a 400 g batch is wasted

cons.claim: Bands treat all sugars as sucrose although substitutes change both sweetness and structure math
cons.example: swapping 100 g sucrose for 100 g fructose-heavy honey solids browns faster and sets softer at the identical sugar percentage, so an in-band formula still misbehaves

cons.claim: Pure-fat accounting understates the functional role of milk solids in butter
cons.example: replacing 227 g butter with 184 g clarified butter matches pure fat exactly yet loses the water and milk solids that drove creaming aeration, dropping cake volume by roughly a tenth

failure_modes: quoting butter mass as fat mass and overstating fat by about 20%
approving sugar at 120% without checking the shortening/mixing precondition
acceptance_tests: the cookie audit reproduces butter 227/280 = 81% and sugars 300/280 = 107%, both flagged against the cookie bands with the spread consequence named
revisit_triggers: a non-sucrose sweetener or non-butter fat enters the formula
hydration sits at top of band while sugar also exceeds 100%

base.update_signal: a sweetener or fat with different functional math becomes a recurring ingredient in audited formulas

nodes.definition: Hold salt at 1.8-2.2% of the flour basis for breads and 1-2% for cakes and cookies (where sugar masks perception): on 500 g flour that is 9-11 g for bread. The band is tight because the palate resolves roughly 0.3-point deviations: 1.5% reads flat, 2.5% reads salted. The dominant real-world corruption is crystal geometry, not intent: table salt packs about 6 g/tsp, Morton kosher about 4.8 g/tsp, Diamond Crystal kosher about 2.8 g/tsp, so '2 tsp salt' spans 5.6-12 g — 1.1% to 2.4% on 500 g flour, i.e. the same written line lands under band with one brand and over band with another. Salt also arrives hidden in salted butter (about 1.5-2 g per 100 g), which on a 227 g butter cake contributes about 3.9 g — roughly 1% of a 360 g flour basis before any salt line is measured.

included: the 1.8-2.2% bread band and 1-2% sweet-goods band

pros.claim: A mass band plus crystal table converts the most complained-about home error into one lookup
pros.example: diagnosing a 'twice as salty as last time' loaf instantly as a Diamond-to-table brand switch at constant teaspoons

pros.claim: Hidden-salt accounting keeps swapped butter from double-salting
pros.example: netting out 3.9 g when salted butter replaces unsalted in a 227 g butter formula keeps total salt at 2.0% instead of 3.1%

cons.claim: One band cannot serve products where salt is functional rather than seasoning
cons.example: bagel boiling and pretzel formulas legitimately run interior salt near 2.5% plus surface salt, which the band flags as defects

cons.claim: Perception-based band edges shift with sugar and acid context
cons.example: 2.0% salt tastes correct in a lean loaf but reads visibly salty in a 20% sugar enriched dough where expectations differ

failure_modes: converting a volume salt line with the wrong crystal constant and dosing 0.5x or 2x the band
ignoring salted-butter salt so the formula lands about 1 point over band
acceptance_tests: the crystal check reproduces: 2 tsp Diamond Crystal = 5.6 g = 1.1% on 500 g flour (under band) while 2 tsp table salt = 12 g = 2.4% (over band)
revisit_triggers: a salted-fat or brined ingredient (miso, soy, olives) enters the formula
the salt brand or crystal in the pantry changes

base.update_signal: a functional-salt product family (bagels, pretzels) enters scope or a crystal constant is re-measured off-table

nodes.definition: Budget chemical lift at 3-4% of flour in baking-powder-equivalent, then split it by acidity: baking soda is 3-3.5x as potent as double-acting powder (powder is only about 28-30% NaHCO3 plus acid salts), and soda must be matched to acid or it survives as soapy, yellowing residue. Allocation order: (1) inventory formula acids — about 2.3 g soda neutralizes 245 g (1 cup) of buttermilk or yogurt, and natural (non-Dutched) cocoa wants very roughly 1 g soda per 30-40 g cocoa, while Dutch-process cocoa (pH about 7-8) wants none; (2) convert allocated soda to powder-equivalent at 3-3.5x; (3) top up with powder to land total lift in band. Worked split: 250 g flour + 245 g buttermilk takes 2.3 g soda = 8.05 g powder-equivalent = 3.2% of flour, already in band, so add at most 1-2 g powder (0.4-0.8%) — a recipe that keeps its full original powder dose after a buttermilk swap is over-leavened by about a third.

included: acid inventory constants (buttermilk, yogurt, natural cocoa)

pros.claim: Allocating soda to measured acid predicts both lift and flavor defects in one pass
pros.example: a soda-only formula with Dutch cocoa is flagged for soapy residue and no first-rise acid before baking, not after tasting

pros.claim: The powder-equivalent unit makes mixed systems auditable as one number
pros.example: 2.3 g soda + 1.5 g powder books as 9.55 g equivalent = 3.8% on 250 g flour, one band check instead of two incomparable lines

cons.claim: Acid constants for real ingredients are far looser than the soda chemistry they feed
cons.example: buttermilk acidity varies with culture and age — a fresh carton may need closer to 1.7 g soda per 245 g while a week-old one needs 2.6 g — so the 2.3 g constant can misallocate by 30% either way

cons.claim: The band ignores dissolved-sugar and batter-viscosity effects on gas retention
cons.example: 3.5% equivalent that domes a muffin correctly will over-inflate and collapse a thin 105%-hydration pancake batter that cannot hold the gas

failure_modes: swapping milk to buttermilk without moving lift from powder to soda, leaving acid unneutralized and the crumb dense and tangy
counting soda grams as powder grams and under-leavening by a factor of about 3
acceptance_tests: the worked split reproduces: 245 g buttermilk takes 2.3 g soda = 8.05 g powder-equivalent = 3.2% on 250 g flour, with top-up capped at band
any soda line in an audited formula traces to a named acid or is flagged
revisit_triggers: an acidic swap (buttermilk, yogurt, honey, natural cocoa, brown sugar shift) enters the formula
a bake shows soapy flavor or dense crumb at an in-band equivalent dose

base.update_signal: a measured neutralization test revises an acid constant, or a new habitual acid ingredient needs a soda coefficient

nodes.definition: Convert between batter mass and volume with class priors stated in g/mL at panning: creamed/butter cake batter 0.85-1.0 (well-creamed toward 0.85, under-creamed toward 1.0), foam and sponge batters 0.45-0.6 (genoise about 0.45-0.5, chiffon about 0.5-0.6), bread and enriched doughs 1.1-1.2, cookie dough 1.0-1.1, and water = 1.0 as the reference. Volume = mass / density, so the same 800 g reads 889 mL as creamed batter at 0.9 but 1600 mL as foam at 0.5 — a 1.8x difference that decides whether a pan overflows. Priors are the planning default only; the specific-gravity cup test measures the real value, and a measured SG always replaces the prior in downstream depth and fill math.

included: the four class density bands with sub-class leanings

pros.claim: Priors make pan planning possible before anything is mixed
pros.example: sizing pans for a 1200 g foam batter at 0.5 g/mL (2400 mL) correctly books two 9-in rounds instead of the one pan a mass-only glance suggests

pros.claim: Sub-class leanings encode mixing state, adding diagnostic power
pros.example: a creamed batter measuring 1.02 g/mL against the 0.85-1.0 band diagnoses broken or under-creamed emulsion before the pan is filled

cons.claim: Density is the least stable constant in the KB because it encodes technique, not composition
cons.example: the identical pound cake formula measures 0.82 g/mL after 8 minutes of stand-mixer creaming and 1.05 g/mL after 2 minutes by hand — the prior band cannot cover both bakers

cons.claim: Priors drift within a session as chemical leavening works
cons.example: a soda-active batter at 0.92 g/mL at mix time reads about 0.85 after 20 minutes of bench time, so late-panned layers run shallower than computed

failure_modes: applying the creamed prior (0.9) to a foam batter (0.5) and under-sizing pan volume by almost half
treating the prior as truth after an SG measurement contradicts it
acceptance_tests: given class and mass, volume computes as mass/density and reproduces 800 g at 0.9 = 889 mL and 800 g at 0.5 = 1600 mL
revisit_triggers: a measured SG departs from the class band by more than 0.1
mixing method or mixer hardware changes for a recurring formula

base.update_signal: accumulated SG measurements for a class consistently sit outside its prior band

nodes.definition: Compute pan capacity and area from geometry: round pans V = pi x r^2 x h and A = pi x r^2; rectangles V = L x W x h. Standard anchors (2-in/5.08 cm walls unless noted): 8-in round = 324 cm^2 area, about 1650 mL (7.0 cups); 9-in round = 410 cm^2, about 2085 mL (8.8 cups); 9x13-in = 3835 mL (16.2 cups); 8.5x4.5x2.75-in loaf = about 1724 mL (7.3 cups). Area ratios drive rescaling: 9-in/8-in round = (4.5/4)^2 = 1.27, so 'same recipe, one inch bigger pan' means 27% more batter at equal depth, not a rounding error. Charts lie for flared and decorative pans — the ground truth is a water fill: weigh the water the pan holds to the brim (1 g = 1 mL) and use that volume whenever it differs from the chart by more than about 5%.

included: V and A formulas for rounds, rectangles, loaves
excluded: heat-transfer differences by pan material and color

pros.claim: Geometry converts pan questions from folklore to arithmetic
pros.example: two 8-in rounds (2 x 1650 mL) vs one 9x13 (3835 mL) resolves as a near-exact volume match (3300 vs 3835 mL, 14% short) instead of a guess

pros.claim: Water-fill calibration absorbs the entire nonstandard-pan universe with one kitchen-scale procedure
pros.example: a flared brioche mold measuring 1420 mL by water fill overrides a chart's 1650 mL and prevents a 16% overfill

cons.claim: Brim volume is not usable volume, and the gap varies by pan type
cons.example: a straight-walled 2085 mL 9-in round accepts a 2/3 fill of 1390 mL, but a bundt with a center core loses additional effective area near the core where batter climbs unevenly

cons.claim: Nominal pan sizes overstate true dimensions inconsistently by brand
cons.example: many '9-in' rounds measure 8.75 in inside the rolled rim, silently shrinking area by 5-6% against the anchor table

failure_modes: using nominal chart volume for a flared or decorative pan and overfilling
comparing pans by diameter instead of area, so 8-in to 9-in reads 'about the same' when it is +27%
acceptance_tests: anchor recomputation holds: 9-in round area = pi x 11.43^2 = 410 cm^2 and volume = 410 x 5.08 = about 2085 mL
revisit_triggers: a pan enters use whose water-fill differs from chart volume by more than 5%
a recipe targets a tube, bundt, or novelty geometry

base.update_signal: a recurring pan's measured water-fill contradicts the anchor table or its nominal size

nodes.definition: Cap panned volume as a fraction of brim volume, leaving headroom for the 1.5-2x in-pan rise: creamed/butter cakes 1/2-2/3 full; muffins and cupcakes 2/3-3/4; quick-bread loaves about 2/3; foam cakes in ungreased tube pans up to 3/4 (the batter climbs the walls and the tube, and a greased pan removes its ladder — a foam batter panned in a greased round at 3/4 both overflows and collapses); yeast pan loaves are panned so proofed dough crests about 1 in / 2.5 cm above the rim before baking. Fill = (mass / density) / pan volume, so the check is one division after the density prior is fixed: 1000 g creamed batter at 0.9 g/mL in a 2085 mL 9-in round = 1111/2085 = 53% — legal; the same mass in a 1650 mL 8-in round = 67% — at the ceiling, and any extra batter is diverted, not squeezed in.

pros.claim: A numeric ceiling converts overflow from a surprise into a pre-mix veto
pros.example: computing 78% fill for a doubled muffin batch in the same tin forces the second tin decision before batter is wasted on a smoking oven floor

pros.claim: Class-specific ceilings capture opposite risks in one rule form
pros.example: the same 3/4 number that is safe for cupcakes is an overflow verdict for a creamed layer, and the rule table encodes that without per-recipe judgment

cons.claim: Ceilings assume typical leavening; they misjudge under- or over-leavened formulas
cons.example: a dense 1.5%-equivalent pound cake filled to 55% bakes a sad short layer that the 2/3 ceiling said was fine, because the real rise was 1.2x not 1.8x

cons.claim: Underfill is a real defect the ceiling language hides
cons.example: a 9-in layer at 30% fill bakes shallow and overdone at the edges before the center sets, yet 'under the ceiling' sounds like a pass

failure_modes: filling a foam batter in a greased pan to tube-pan levels and losing both height and containment
reading the ceiling as a target and thinning layers to absurdity
acceptance_tests: fill computes as (mass/density)/brim and reproduces 1000 g at 0.9 in 2085 mL = 53%
each class row carries both a floor (about 40-50% of ceiling class-adjusted) and a ceiling so underfill is also flagged
revisit_triggers: measured rise for a recurring formula departs from the 1.5-2x assumption
a tube, bundt, or ungreased-wall geometry changes the effective ceiling

base.update_signal: observed rise multipliers for a class drift outside 1.5-2x and the ceiling needs re-centering

nodes.definition: Compute raw batter depth as depth = mass / (density x pan area) — the single formula that links the formulation ledger to the oven's thermal problem. Worked anchor: 800 g creamed batter at 0.9 g/mL in an 8-in round (area = pi x 10.16^2 = 324 cm^2) occupies 889 mL and stands 889/324 = 2.7 cm deep — 54% of a 5.08 cm pan, inside the creamed ceiling. The same 800 g as foam at 0.5 g/mL stands 4.9 cm in that pan (97% fill — veto). Depth, not mass, is what the oven sees: bake-time scaling, doneness gradients, and edge-overbake all key on this number, so depth is computed and recorded for every bake, making later time predictions and cross-pan transfers table lookups instead of re-derivations.

included: the depth = m/(rho x A) formula
depth as the handoff variable to time scaling

pros.claim: One formula unifies formulation and baking decisions through a single physical variable
pros.example: a recipe moved from a 9x13 (2.2 cm deep) to a loaf pan (6.8 cm deep) is immediately known to be a 3x-depth, different-exponent bake, not 'same batter, same time'

pros.claim: Recorded depths turn every past bake into a calibration point
pros.example: knowing the house brownie bakes correctly at 2.5 cm/32 min anchors the time estimate when the same batter goes in at 3.2 cm

cons.claim: The formula inherits every upstream error multiplicatively
cons.example: a density prior off by 0.1 (0.9 assumed, 0.8 real) plus a nominal-size pan 5% small compounds to a depth estimate about 17% shallow — enough to flip a fill verdict at the ceiling

cons.claim: Uniform-depth math misdescribes stiff doughs and mounded batters
cons.example: a cookie-dough slab pressed into a 9x13 sits mounded at 2.8 cm center and 2.0 cm edge; the computed 2.4 cm 'depth' exists nowhere in the pan

failure_modes: dividing by brim volume instead of area and reporting a fill fraction as a depth
quoting depth from the prior after a measured SG contradicted it
acceptance_tests: the anchor reproduces: 800 g at 0.9 g/mL over 324 cm^2 = 2.7 cm and flips to 4.9 cm at 0.5 g/mL
every recorded bake carries mass, density source (prior or measured), area, and computed depth
revisit_triggers: a measured SG replaces the prior for the batter in question
the pan's true area is re-measured (rolled rim, flare) and differs from nominal

base.update_signal: compounded prior-plus-geometry error is caught flipping a fill or time verdict, forcing measured inputs

nodes.definition: Scale bake time with depth to the 0.8-1.1 power — near-linear, and explicitly NOT the super-linear depth-squared law that pure conduction into an inert slab would suggest, because evaporation, convection within the batter, and rising crumb porosity flatten the response. Doubling depth multiplies time by 2^0.8 to 2^1.1 = 1.74-2.14x; moving a 2.5 cm sheet-pan batter into a 7 cm-deep loaf (2.8x depth) multiplies time by 2.8^0.8 to 2.8^1.1 = 2.3-3.1x. Width at constant depth barely matters: an 8-in and a 9-in round filled to the same 2.7 cm bake in nearly the same time (edge effects only), which is why rescaling at constant depth is the preferred transfer. Temperature is not a free compensator — dropping 15-20 C to protect a deep bake's surface adds roughly 15-25% time. The exponent estimate only schedules the first check; the thermometer owns the verdict.

included: the depth^0.8-1.1 law and its two worked ratios

pros.claim: The exponent kills the two dominant folk errors in one rule — time-per-volume and time-per-mass
pros.example: a doubled batch split into two identical pans bakes in the original time (same depth), not 2x, and the law says so before the first dry cake

pros.claim: Bounded exponents give honest uncertainty instead of false precision
pros.example: quoting 46-62 min for a 2x-depth transfer of a 26-32 min bake (26 x 1.74 = 45 to 32 x 2.14 = 68... tightened by the house calibration point to 46-62) sets the probe schedule realistically

cons.claim: The exponent band is fit to typical home depths (1.5-8 cm) and degrades outside it
cons.example: a 12 cm-deep panettone-style bake develops a crust-insulation regime where effective exponent creeps above 1.1 and the model underestimates time by 15%+

cons.claim: Depth scaling assumes the surface can survive the extra minutes
cons.example: a high-sugar (110%) batter taken from 2.5 to 7 cm hits its 2.6x time with a surface 20 shades past mahogany unless temperature drops, which the depth law alone does not command

failure_modes: scaling time by volume ratio so a same-depth doubled batch gets doubled minutes and bakes to sawdust
trusting the computed time over a thermometer reading that says the center is 8 C short
acceptance_tests: the two anchors reproduce: 2x depth = 1.74-2.14x time and 2.8x depth = 2.3-3.1x time
every time estimate is emitted with its exponent bounds and a first-check time at about 90% of the low estimate
revisit_triggers: a logged bake misses the predicted window by more than 20%, demanding a house-specific exponent refit
a transfer leaves the 1.5-8 cm calibrated depth range

base.update_signal: logged time-vs-depth pairs for one oven support a tighter house exponent than the 0.8-1.1 prior

nodes.definition: Doneness is a center-temperature fact, not a clock fact: butter and oil cakes are done at 93-99 C (200-210 F), lean breads at 96-99 C (205-210 F), enriched breads at 88-93 C (190-200 F, richer doughs finish lower because fat and sugar depress the set point and keep browning ahead of the interior), fudgy brownies at 87-91 C, and baked custards/cheesecakes at 65-70 C center with carryover finishing the set. Every time estimate from the depth law is a scheduling device for the first probe; the thermometer reading at the geometric center (probe from the side for shallow layers to avoid a vent hole) is the release gate. Carryover matters at depth: a 7 cm loaf center climbs 2-4 C after pull, so deep bakes exit at the bottom of their window.

pros.claim: A temperature gate is transferable across every oven, pan, and altitude quirk the time model cannot see
pros.example: the same 96 C target releases the sandwich loaf correctly in a fast convection oven at 24 min and a cold spot-prone gas oven at 33 min

pros.claim: Class targets convert 'toothpick ambiguity' into a number a beginner can act on
pros.example: a chocolate cake whose crumbs always look wet on the pick releases confidently at 96 C instead of being baked 10 minutes 'to be safe'

cons.claim: Temperature is nearly flat in the last minutes of moist bakes, so the gate has poor resolution exactly at the decision point
cons.example: a custard cake center crawls from 97 to 99 C over 8 minutes; within that plateau the thermometer cannot distinguish just-set from slightly overbaked, and texture cues must break the tie

cons.claim: Thin items finish too fast and too shallow to probe meaningfully
cons.example: a 1 cm cookie's center outruns any probe insertion; doneness there is color and set, and the temperature gate simply does not apply

failure_modes: pulling an enriched bread at the lean-bread 99 C target and drying it
probing off-center (near a pan wall) and releasing a raw-centered deep loaf 5 C early
acceptance_tests: each product class carries a numeric center-temp window plus a carryover offset, and the deep-bake rule (exit at window bottom above about 5 cm depth) is stated
revisit_triggers: a class repeatedly reads done-by-temp but underbaked-by-texture (plateau problem)
a new product family needs its own window

base.update_signal: a doneness window is contradicted by repeated texture outcomes at in-window pulls for one class

nodes.definition: Transfer a recipe between pans by holding depth constant and scaling every ingredient by the area ratio: 8-in to 9-in round scales by (4.5/4)^2 = 1.27; 9-in to 8-in by 0.79; one 9-in round to a 9x13 by 758/410... corrected to true areas: 9x13 = 758 cm^2 vs 9-in round 410 cm^2 = 1.85x. Constant depth means bake time and temperature carry over nearly unchanged — the whole point of scaling by area. If instead the batter mass is held and depth changes, the transfer must run the depth law: the unscaled 8-in recipe poured into a 9-in pan sits at 2.7 x 0.79 = 2.1 cm, and time drops by (0.79)^0.8-1.1 = 0.77-0.83x, or the layer overbakes at the original timer. Leavening and salt scale linearly with the rest of the formula in home batch ranges (0.25x-4x); no percentage is re-derived, only masses.

included: the changed-depth fallback via the time law
linear scaling of all baker's percentages in home ranges

pros.claim: Constant-depth transfer preserves the one variable the oven cares about, so times survive the move
pros.example: scaling the 8-in recipe x1.27 into the 9-in keeps 2.7 cm depth and the 30-minute bake, versus the unscaled pour that bakes 5 minutes fast and dry

pros.claim: Area-ratio math exposes deceptive 'one inch' changes
pros.example: 8-in to 10-in rounds is (5/4)^2 = 1.56x — a half-recipe more, not 'a little extra', and the formula shows it in one line

cons.claim: Constant-depth scaling silently changes crust-to-crumb ratio through the wall perimeter
cons.example: the same batter at 2.7 cm in a 9x13 has proportionally less hot wall per gram than in two 8-in rounds, browning edges less even at identical depth and time

cons.claim: Linear leavening scaling frays at the extremes of the home range
cons.example: a 4x batch in one deep pan is no longer a constant-depth transfer at all, and quadrupled soda in a now-6 cm-deep slab produces a coarse, alkaline center the area rule never anticipated

failure_modes: scaling by diameter ratio (9/8 = 1.125) instead of area ratio (1.27) and under-filling by 11%
holding batter mass constant across pans while also holding the timer constant
acceptance_tests: the transfer table reproduces 8-to-9-in = 1.27x, 9-to-8-in = 0.79x, 9-in round-to-9x13 = 1.85x, each with the constant-depth time carryover stated
revisit_triggers: a transfer changes both pan area and target depth at once
batch scale leaves the 0.25x-4x linear range

base.update_signal: a constant-depth transfer changes bake outcome enough to implicate perimeter effects, warranting a shape-correction term

nodes.definition: After any substitution, run the closure ledger: enumerate what the swap adds and removes in water, fat, sugar, salt, and acid, then adjust other lines until every band the swap touched is back in range. Worked closures: (1) honey for 100 g sugar — use 120 g honey (about 96 g sugars + 20.4 g water at 17%), so cut added liquid by about 20 g and note honey's mild acidity for the leavening split; (2) oil for 100 g butter — butter is about 81% fat/16% water, so use 81 g oil + 16 g water (or milk) to hold both fat and hydration budgets, accepting the loss of creaming aeration (density rises, so re-measure SG); (3) buttermilk for 240 g milk — water is nearly identical (210 vs 211 g) but acidity now demands about 2.3 g soda, retiring about 8 g of powder-equivalent from the powder line; (4) salted for unsalted butter on 227 g — subtract about 3.9 g from the salt line. A swap without closure is not a substitution; it is a new, unaudited formula.

included: the four worked closures (honey, oil, buttermilk, salted butter)
the rule that every touched band is re-checked
excluded: allergen-driven redesign beyond 1:1-plus-closure (owned by dietary math)

pros.claim: Closure catches the second-order effect that folk substitution tables omit
pros.example: most tables say 'use 3/4 cup honey per cup sugar' but not 'remove 20 g liquid', and the ledger books exactly that line, preventing the gummy stripe over the base

pros.claim: Ledger discipline makes swaps composable
pros.example: honey + buttermilk together book their water, acid, and lift moves as independent lines that sum, instead of interacting invisibly

cons.claim: Mass closure cannot restore lost function, and pretending it can is the ledger's blind spot
cons.example: the 81 g oil + 16 g water closure balances every band yet the cake still loses about 10% volume because creamed butter's air cells, not its fat grams, did the leavening

cons.claim: Chained swaps accumulate rounding into a real drift
cons.example: three sequential closures each rounded to 5 g can leave hydration 12 g (5 points on 250 g flour) off the audited value while every individual step looked closed

failure_modes: swapping honey in without removing its water and exiting the hydration band by 8 points
closing mass budgets while ignoring the acid ledger so the leavening split is silently wrong
acceptance_tests: each worked closure recomputes: 120 g honey imports 20.4 g water; 100 g butter = 81 g oil + 16 g water; 240 g buttermilk moves 2.3 g soda / retires about 8 g powder-equivalent; salted butter nets -3.9 g salt on 227 g
post-swap, every touched band re-audits in range or the swap is flagged as a reformulation
revisit_triggers: two or more swaps stack in one formula
a swap crosses functional class (solid to liquid fat, sugar to liquid sweetener)

base.update_signal: a common swap's closure constants (honey water fraction, butter fat fraction) are re-measured off the table values

nodes.definition: Treat 'no eggs' as arithmetic, not vibes: each removed 50 g egg deletes 37.5 g water, about 6.3 g protein, and 5 g fat. The water is replaceable gram-for-gram (milk at 87.5% water: 43 g milk carries 37.6 g), but the coagulating protein is not — egg protein sets crumb around 70-85 C, and without it the formula's tolerance for free water shrinks, so the class hydration ceiling tightens by 5-10 points (a 95-110% pour batter becomes effectively 90-100%). Binders buy back some ceiling: a flax egg (7 g ground flax + 45 g water per egg) or 60 g yogurt add gel viscosity but zero thermoset protein — and note the flax egg brings 45 g of free water against the egg's 37.5 g of protein-bound water, a +7.5 g wet shift per egg that must be booked. Practical corollary: eggless conversions succeed most often on formulas already sitting at the bottom of their hydration band, and the math says exactly why.

excluded: vegan dairy/fat swaps in general (plain closure ledger)

pros.claim: The tightened ceiling predicts which recipes will survive egg removal before any test bake
pros.example: a 96%-hydration butter cake clears the 100% eggless ceiling and converts cleanly, while a 108% formula is flagged for a mandatory liquid cut of about 20 g per 250 g flour

pros.claim: Per-egg component accounting scales to partial constraints
pros.example: a yolk-only restriction (allergy to white protein) books just the 27 g white water and its albumin set, leaving yolk lecithin emulsification in place

cons.claim: The 5-10 point tightening is the softest constant in this KB, fit from heterogeneous home results
cons.example: starch-rich formulas (30%+ of flour as cake flour or added starch) gelatinize enough to hold near the original ceiling, while lean all-purpose crumbs need the full 10-point cut — one number cannot serve both

cons.claim: Ceiling math says nothing about aeration lost with the egg foam
cons.example: an eggless sponge conversion can be perfectly in-band on water yet rise 40% short because whipped egg was the leavening system, a failure the hydration ledger cannot see

failure_modes: replacing egg mass with milk 1:1 and calling it closed while the crumb sets gummy at the old ceiling
booking a flax egg as water-neutral when it adds 7.5 g free water per egg
acceptance_tests: a conversion shows per-egg lines (37.5 g water out, binder water in, net wet shift) and an explicit tightened ceiling with the formula's position against it
revisit_triggers: a binder with real thermoset behavior (chickpea/lupin protein isolates) enters the toolbox
logged eggless bakes bracket the true tightening for a class more tightly than 5-10 points

base.update_signal: accumulated eggless bake logs pin the ceiling tightening for a product class to a narrower interval

nodes.definition: Allocate one batch across layers and tiers by pan area at equal depth: 6/8/10-in rounds have areas 182/324/507 cm^2, ratio 36:64:100 (diameter squared), with the elegant check that a 6-in plus an 8-in layer take exactly one 10-in layer's batter (36+64=100). At 2.7 cm depth and 0.9 g/mL, that is about 443 g, 788 g, and 1231 g per layer — a full three-tier, two-layers-each build books 2 x (443+788+1231) = 4924 g of batter, sized before the mixer starts. Equal depth is the governing choice because it lets all tiers share one oven at one time-temperature; unequal depths re-invoke the depth-time law per tier. Frosting and filling scale differently — filling scales with layer area, coating frosting with surface area (top + sides = pi r^2 + 2 pi r x height) — so a 10-in tier needs about 2.8x the 6-in's filling but only about 2x its side coating... computed: sides 2 pi x 12.7 x 10 cm vs 2 pi x 7.62 x 10 cm = 1.67x, and the plan books them as separate lines.

pros.claim: Area allocation converts multi-tier planning into one batch-size equation
pros.example: the 4924 g three-tier total tells the baker it is a 2x run of a 2500 g-batch recipe before any pan is buttered

pros.claim: The 36+64=100 identity gives a zero-arithmetic sanity check at the bench
pros.example: batter left after filling the 6-in and 8-in should exactly fill the 10-in; visible surplus or deficit flags a depth error immediately

cons.claim: Equal-depth policy forces compromise bake times when tier compositions differ
cons.example: a 10-in fruit-heavy tier and a 6-in plain tier at the same depth still finish 10+ minutes apart because load, not depth, separates them — the area math cannot see filling density

cons.claim: Area ratios ignore batter losses that hit small pans proportionally harder
cons.example: a fixed 60 g bowl-and-scraper residue is 13% of a 6-in layer's 443 g but 5% of a 10-in's 1231 g, so the smallest tier consistently runs shallow unless residue is booked per pan

failure_modes: allocating by diameter (6:8:10) instead of area (36:64:100) and starving the large tier by a third
sizing frosting by batter mass so tall thin tiers run short on side coating
acceptance_tests: the allocation reproduces 443/788/1231 g at 2.7 cm and 0.9 g/mL and the 36+64=100 identity is stated as the bench check
revisit_triggers: tier depths are deliberately unequal for effect
a tier's composition (fruit load, foam class) departs from its siblings

base.update_signal: a tier build logs systematic shallow small tiers, forcing per-pan residue lines in the allocation

nodes.definition: Plan raw batch size from target finished mass by inverting the loss chain: bake loss (evaporation) runs 10-15% for pan loaves (about 12% typical), 15-20% for free-standing baguette-shaped loaves (more surface per gram), 8-12% for cakes and quick breads, and 10-15% for cookies; mixing and transfer residue costs another 2-4% (a fixed 40-80 g per home batch, hitting small batches harder); divider/portioning trim adds 1-2% when dough is scaled into pieces. The formula is multiplicative: raw = target / ((1 - bake loss) x (1 - residue)). Worked: a 900 g baked sandwich loaf at 12% bake loss needs 900/0.88 = 1023 g of panned dough; wanting that from a batch with 3% residue means mixing 1023/0.97 = 1055 g. Yield math also runs forward for portion counts: 1055 g mixed dough yields 1023 g panned = 900 g baked = 18 slices at 50 g, and every arrow in that chain is checkable by scale.

excluded: staling and storage moisture loss after cooling

pros.claim: Inverting losses up front ends the chronic underweight-output surprise
pros.example: the baker who always wondered why the '900 g recipe' yields a 792 g loaf sees the 12% bake loss line and mixes 1023 g instead

pros.claim: A checkable mass chain localizes process faults
pros.example: panned 1020 g but baked out at 858 g (16% loss) against a 12% expectation points at the oven or an overlong bake, not the formula

cons.claim: Bake loss is a function of time, temperature, and geometry, so class constants misprice unusual bakes
cons.example: the same dough loses 11% as a lidded pullman and 19% as a free-form batard; one 'bread' constant is wrong for one of them by up to 8 points

cons.claim: Fixed-percent residue models misstate the fixed-mass reality at batch extremes
cons.example: a 300 g single-loaf test batch loses the same 50 g bowl residue as a 3 kg batch — 17% vs 1.7% — and a 3% assumption is wrong at both ends

failure_modes: quoting the recipe's raw mass as its yield and under-delivering by 12-20%
double-counting loss by applying bake loss to the mixed mass instead of the panned mass
acceptance_tests: the worked chain reproduces 900/0.88 = 1023 g panned and 1023/0.97 = 1055 g mixed, and forward and inverse runs agree within 1%
revisit_triggers: a logged bake-loss measurement departs from the class constant by more than 3 points
batch size moves outside the range where percent residue approximates fixed-mass residue

base.update_signal: logged pre/post-bake weighings revise a class bake-loss constant or expose lid/shape dependence

nodes.definition: Verify the density assumption with the cup test before committing batter to pans: tare a cup, fill level with batter, weigh; fill the same cup level with water, weigh; SG = batter mass / water mass. A 236.6 mL cup holding 213 g of batter reads SG 0.90. Targets by class: well-creamed butter cake 0.80-0.95, foam/genoise 0.45-0.55, muffin batter about 0.9-1.0. The test costs one minute and one dirty cup, and it is the only step in the KB that measures rather than assumes — a reading outside the class band is an immediate instruction: keep creaming (too heavy), stop folding (foam too heavy = deflating; too light for the formula = underfolded flour pockets), or re-run pan fill and depth with the measured value. The measured SG supersedes the prior in all downstream depth, fill, and tier math for that batch, and logged SG values per recipe become the house prior over time.

included: the tare-fill-weigh procedure and SG formula

pros.claim: One measurement collapses the KB's widest uncertainty (density) to near zero for the batch at hand
pros.example: measuring 0.86 instead of the assumed 0.95 revises a planned 62% fill to 68% — over ceiling — and reroutes 150 g of batter to a cupcake before the oven finds out

pros.claim: SG trends are an early drift alarm for technique and ingredients
pros.example: a house cake logging 0.88, 0.89, 0.97 across three bakes flags the new margarine or the tired mixer paddle before customers taste it

cons.claim: The test destroys sample and time exactly when foams are most perishable
cons.example: scooping and leveling a cup of genoise batter pops enough foam that the batter returned to the bowl is measurably heavier, and a 3-minute delay costs a further 0.02-0.04 SG

cons.claim: Cup-fill technique injects its own 3-5% noise
cons.example: tapping the cup to settle a creamed batter reads 0.93 where a no-tap fill of the same batter reads 0.89, straddling an action threshold

failure_modes: skipping the water weighing and dividing by nominal cup volume with a mis-set tare, shifting every SG by a constant error
measuring after the pans are filled, when the answer can no longer change the plan
acceptance_tests: the procedure reproduces SG = 213/236.6 = 0.90 for the worked cup, and each class threshold maps to a named corrective action
revisit_triggers: measured SG for a recurring recipe stabilizes tightly enough to replace the class prior
a foam product needs a gentler (smaller-vessel) variant of the test

base.update_signal: logged SG history for a recipe becomes tight enough to promote to its house prior, or the test procedure changes vessel

nodes.definition: Run the complete pre-bake audit as one pass over the ledger: (1) convert all volumes to grams with recorded assumptions; (2) fix the flour basis; (3) restate in baker's percent; (4) classify the product; (5) sum hidden plus added water against the hydration band; (6) check fat, sugar, salt, and leavening bands, splitting powder/soda by the acid inventory; (7) plan pan, depth, fill, time, and yield. Worked audit — 1-2-3-4 cake (360 g flour, 400 g sugar, 227 g butter, 200 g egg, 240 g milk, 13.8 g powder, 6 g salt): sugar 111% (top of band), butter 63% (in band, about 51% pure fat), hydration 396/360 = 110% (top of band), leavening 3.8% (in band), salt 1.7% (low side, fine for a sweet crumb). Verdict: legal but zero-headroom — the audit's product is not just pass/fail but a headroom report saying which single band any future swap will break first (here: hydration). Every flag names its line, its band, and the gram change that would re-enter band, so the user decides with numbers instead of adjectives.

pros.claim: A fixed audit order guarantees errors are caught at their cheapest stage
pros.example: the scooped-flour conversion error surfaces at step 1 as a bracketed 360-426 g flour range, before it could masquerade as a hydration-band failure at step 5

pros.claim: Headroom reporting turns a static audit into swap-planning intelligence
pros.example: knowing the 1-2-3-4 cake has zero wet headroom but 0.4% leavening headroom tells the user a honey swap needs closure while a buttermilk swap has room

cons.claim: A full audit on every minor tweak trains users to skip auditing entirely
cons.example: re-running seven steps because vanilla went from 5 to 8 g is busywork; without a materiality floor (skip when the change is under 0.5% of flour and touches no band within 3 points of its edge), compliance decays in a week

cons.claim: Band-based verdicts inherit every band's own blind spots simultaneously
cons.example: the audit passes a formula whose milk-vs-water bound-water quirk and non-sucrose sweetener both sit in individually known blind spots, compounding into a wrong pass verdict with high stated confidence

failure_modes: auditing percentages before fixing the flour basis, invalidating every subsequent number
reporting pass/fail without headroom so the next swap decision is made blind
acceptance_tests: the 1-2-3-4 worked audit reproduces all five quoted percentages (111, 63, 110, 3.8, 1.7) within rounding
every emitted flag carries line, band, and a gram-denominated correction
revisit_triggers: any upstream band or constant changes value
audit skip-rate climbs, indicating the materiality floor is mis-set

base.update_signal: an upstream constant or band revision propagates, or audit compliance data forces a materiality-floor change

edges.why_related: the flour=100 convention is meaningless until the basis rules say which masses sum to the denominator
class bands are stated in baker's percent, so the convention must exist before bands can be written
hydration is a percent of the flour basis, and preferment/cocoa rulings change the denominator directly
total hydration is uncomputable until egg/dairy/butter/puree water fractions convert wet ingredients to water grams
the class decides which hydration band (95-110 pour vs 60-75 lean bread) the summed water is judged against
fat and sugar bands are class-conditional; the same 107% sugar passes cookies and fails breads
the 3-4% lift band applies to chemically leavened classes and not to yeast-structured doughs
density priors are indexed by product class; classification is what selects 0.9 vs 0.5 vs 1.15 g/mL
doneness windows are class-conditional (93-99 C cakes vs 88-93 C enriched bread), so the class call precedes the target
fill fraction divides batter volume by brim volume, which pan geometry or water-fill supplies
the batter volume in the fill quotient comes from mass divided by the class density prior
depth = mass/(density x area) needs the pan's true area from geometry or calibration
the density term in the depth formula is the class prior until a measurement replaces it
the time law scales on depth ratios, so computed depth is its only input variable
area ratios like (4.5/4)^2 = 1.27 are the scaling factors, and they come straight from pan geometry
the changed-depth fallback in pan transfers prices its time consequence through the depth exponent
closure exists to return the hydration ledger to band after a swap moves water in or out
fat and sugar swaps (oil for butter, honey for sugar) are closed against these bands' definitions
acidic swaps re-run the powder/soda allocation, so closure needs the split rules and acid constants
eggless work is the closure ledger plus a structural ceiling correction; the ledger mechanics come first
tier allocation is repeated area-ratio scaling across 6/8/10-in pans at one shared depth
per-tier batter masses must respect each pan's fill ceiling or the plan overfills the smallest tier
the cup test exists to verify or replace the class prior, so the prior bands define its action thresholds
the audit's step 5 is the hydration budget check run inside the fixed seven-step order
the audit's band pass consumes the fat/sugar bands and their carrier-vs-pure-fat accounting
salt band and crystal math are audited at step 6, including hidden salted-butter salt
the audit verifies total powder-equivalent lift and traces every soda gram to a named acid
the audit's step 1 is conversion with recorded assumptions; no later step is valid on volumes
the audit's yield plan inverts bake-loss and residue constants to size the raw batch
the exponent model emits a time window while the thermometer emits a temperature fact, and near the end of a bake they routinely disagree
edges.resolution_rule: the internal-temperature target always wins; the depth-scaled estimate is demoted to scheduling the first probe at about 90% of the low time bound

edges.why_related: a transfer that preserves batch mass into a smaller pan pushes computed fill past the class ceiling, pitting batch integrity against containment
edges.resolution_rule: the fill ceiling wins: cap the pan at its class fill and divert surplus batter to cupcakes or a second pan rather than exceeding the ceiling

edges.why_related: the general class band permits up to 110% water while the eggless structural ceiling tolerates 5-10 points less, so a formula can pass one and fail the other
edges.resolution_rule: when the eggless constraint is active, the tightened ceiling (band minus 5-10 points) overrides the general class band for all wet decisions

edges.why_related: a volume salt line is internally ambiguous across crystals (2.8-6 g/tsp), so the written recipe and the mass band can both claim authority over the salt dose
edges.resolution_rule: mass wins: dose salt in grams against the 1.8-2.2% band using the brand-specific g/tsp constant, and record which crystal the original line assumed

edges.why_related: swaps that carry salt (salted butter at about 1.7 g per 100 g, miso, brined items) must be netted against the salt band inside the closure ledger
a measured SG flows back into the depth formula and re-prices fill and time for the batch that was just measured
creaming fat with sugar entrains the air that sets batter density, so fat/sugar levels and method causally position a batch inside the 0.85-1.0 band
both are narrow percent-of-flour dosing problems (about 2% and 3-4%) where single-gram errors flip outcomes and volume measures are the dominant corruption
every closed swap is followed by a fresh audit pass, because closure fixes touched bands but only the audit re-verifies the whole ledger
longer, deeper bakes evaporate more water, so the time scaling that stretches a bake also pushes bake loss toward the top of its class range

conflict_axes.name: thermometer_vs_timer
conflict_axes.description: The depth-exponent model produces a time window; the internal-temperature gate produces a physical doneness fact; near the pull decision they frequently disagree by several minutes.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: temperature always decides; the model only schedules the first probe at about 90% of the low bound

conflict_axes.name: measured_sg_vs_density_prior
conflict_axes.description: Class density priors enable planning before mixing, but the cup test can contradict them by 0.1+ g/mL on the day, and depth/fill verdicts flip inside that gap.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: priors plan, measurements govern: any SG reading supersedes the prior for that batch and is logged toward a house prior

conflict_axes.name: mass_accuracy_vs_volume_convenience
conflict_axes.description: Grams are unambiguous but cups and spoons are how home recipes are written and how many users want to cook; forcing full conversion costs adoption while tolerating volumes costs correctness.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: convert once at intake with recorded assumptions and bracket ambiguous lines (spooned vs scooped) instead of refusing them

conflict_axes.name: band_compliance_vs_heirloom_fidelity
conflict_axes.description: Budget bands flag a grandmother's proven recipe as out-of-band, but the recipe demonstrably works; silently 'correcting' it destroys trust and sometimes the recipe.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: bands diagnose, users decide: report the deviation, its predicted consequence, and the gram correction, but never auto-rewrite a working formula

conflict_axes.name: pan_fit_vs_batch_integrity
conflict_axes.description: When batter exceeds the fill ceiling of the available pan, either the ceiling breaks (overflow risk) or the batch splits (a second format the baker did not want).
poles: keep the batch whole in one pan
enforce the fill ceiling and divert surplus
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: the ceiling is non-negotiable; divert surplus to cupcakes or a second pan and scale time for the new depth

conflict_axes.name: soda_neutralization_vs_powder_reliability
conflict_axes.description: Soda paired to acid gives better browning and tenderness but depends on loose acid constants; powder is self-contained and reliable but leaves formula acid unneutralized and adds its own salts.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: allocate soda only to acids with known constants (buttermilk, yogurt, natural cocoa) and let powder carry the remainder of the 3-4% band

conflict_axes.name: eggless_moisture_vs_structure
conflict_axes.description: Restoring an egg's 37.5 g of water keeps the crumb moist but the missing thermoset protein cannot hold that water, so moisture parity and structural integrity pull in opposite directions.
poles: replace all removed water for moistness
cut water to protect the weakened set
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: tighten the hydration ceiling 5-10 points, replace water only up to the tightened ceiling, and buy back moisture with binders and fat rather than free water

conflict_axes.name: near_linear_scaling_vs_volume_intuition
conflict_axes.description: Users intuitively scale time with batch volume or mass (double batch = double time), while the physics scales with depth to the 0.8-1.1 power and is width-indifferent.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: teach the two-pan counterexample (doubled batch in two pans bakes in original time) and always quote time as a depth-ratio computation

conflict_axes.name: yield_maximization_vs_doneness
conflict_axes.description: Bake loss is bought yield: pulling earlier or lidding pans keeps grams of water in the product, but the doneness gate demands the center reach temperature whatever the scale says.
poles: bake fully to the temperature gate
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: doneness wins; recover yield upstream by mixing a larger raw batch (target/(1-loss)) instead of shorting the bake

edge_cases.description: A recipe's '2 tsp kosher salt' is measured with Diamond Crystal (2.8 g/tsp) though the author used Morton (4.8 g/tsp), silently under-salting by 42%
edge_cases.trigger: a volume salt line crosses salt brands between author and cook
edge_cases.mitigation: convert to grams against the 1.8-2.2% band using the cook's actual crystal constant and record the assumed brand

edge_cases.description: Scooped-cup flour at 145 g/cup makes a recipe converted at 120 g/cup read 100% hydration when the author's real formula was about 83%
edge_cases.trigger: flour measured by dip-and-sweep is converted with the spooned constant
edge_cases.mitigation: bracket the conversion (120-145 g/cup), audit both ends, and pick the end whose full band profile is coherent

edge_cases.description: A banana bread with 300 g of overripe banana on 250 g flour carries 225 g hidden water (90 points) before any milk, blowing the drop-batter ceiling
edge_cases.trigger: fruit puree mass exceeds roughly half the flour basis
edge_cases.mitigation: book puree water at its constant, cut other liquid to re-enter band, and extend bake time for the wetter crumb via the depth law

edge_cases.description: An 8-in recipe is poured unscaled into a 9-in pan; depth falls 21% and the layer overbakes at the original timer
edge_cases.trigger: pan diameter changes without the 1.27x area rescale
edge_cases.mitigation: scale ingredients by 1.27 for constant depth, or keep the mass and cut time by the 0.77-0.83 factor from the depth law

edge_cases.description: A foam batter (0.5 g/mL) is panned using the creamed prior (0.9), computing 54% fill that is really 97% — overflow and collapse
edge_cases.trigger: density prior selected by habit instead of product class
edge_cases.mitigation: class-check the prior and run the SG cup test whenever the mixing method involves whipped eggs

edge_cases.description: Honey replaces sugar cup-for-cup: 340 g honey for 200 g sugar adds 58 g water and 25% more sweetener mass, exiting two bands at once
edge_cases.trigger: a liquid sweetener swap done by volume without closure
edge_cases.mitigation: swap by sugar-solids mass (120 g honey per 100 g sugar), remove about 20 g liquid per 120 g honey, and re-audit both bands

edge_cases.description: Milk is swapped to buttermilk for tang but the leavening stays all-powder, leaving 245 g of acid unneutralized: dense, sour-edged crumb and pale browning
edge_cases.trigger: an acidic dairy swap without re-running the powder/soda split
edge_cases.mitigation: allocate about 2.3 g soda per 245 g buttermilk, retire about 8 g of powder-equivalent, and confirm total lift stays in the 3-4% band

edge_cases.description: An eggless conversion replaces 100 g of egg with 100 g of milk; the hydration ledger barely moves (87.5% vs 75% water) yet the cake bakes gummy because no protein sets
edge_cases.trigger: egg replacement closed on water mass alone
edge_cases.mitigation: apply the tightened ceiling (minus 5-10 points), add a binder with its water booked, and cut free liquid to the new ceiling

edge_cases.description: Batter waits 45 minutes while the first batch bakes; double-acting powder spends part of its first action and the second batch rises visibly lower at identical mass and depth
edge_cases.trigger: batch baking with a single-oven bottleneck and chemically leavened batter
edge_cases.mitigation: pan all layers before the first bake or re-measure SG on the held batter and accept the recomputed depth and rise

edge_cases.description: A flared 'brioche' mold's chart volume (1650 mL) exceeds its true water-fill (1420 mL) by 16%, so a legal computed fill overflows in practice
edge_cases.trigger: a decorative or flared pan used with nominal chart volume
edge_cases.mitigation: water-fill calibrate any nonstandard pan (1 g = 1 mL to the brim) and use measured volume whenever it differs from chart by over 5%

edge_cases.description: A sheet-pan recipe (2.5 cm deep, 30 min) is baked as one deep loaf (7 cm); volume intuition says 'a bit longer' but the depth law demands 2.3-3.1x the time, and the center stalls raw at the old timer
edge_cases.trigger: a format change that multiplies depth by more than 2x
edge_cases.mitigation: recompute time as ratio^0.8-1.1 (here 69-93 min), drop oven temperature 15-20 C to protect the surface, and release only on center temperature

workflow.action: Convert every recipe line to grams
workflow.description: Apply method-aware constants (flour 120 vs 145 g/cup, salt by crystal, eggs at 50 g) and record each assumption
workflow.artifact: gram-weight mass ledger with conversion assumptions
workflow.gate: no volume-only lines remain and every ambiguous conversion is bracketed with both candidate masses

workflow.description: Sum all flours plus cocoa, fold preferment flour and water into the totals, note whole-grain absorption offsets
workflow.artifact: declared flour basis with preferment bookkeeping
workflow.gate: the basis reproduces the preferment closure (poolish flour and water both booked exactly once)

workflow.action: Restate the formula in baker's percent
workflow.description: Divide every line by the flour basis so all later checks are scale-free percentages
workflow.gate: flour reads exactly 100% and spot-check lines (50 g egg on 250 g = 20%) recompute correctly

workflow.action: Classify the product and select its band set
workflow.description: Assign lean/enriched/pour/drop/cookie/foam from structure-setter and mixing method, not the title
